title: Does Social Media Sentiment Actually Predict Crypto Volatility?
description: My MSc final project at the University of Hertfordshire — comparing GARCH, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LSTM on ten major cryptocurrencies to see whether sentiment data adds real predictive signal beyond price history alone.
content:
Crypto markets are loud in a way few other asset classes are — every price move comes with a wave of social-media chatter, news coverage, and sentiment swings attached to it. The obvious question, and the one my MSc final project set out to actually test rather than assume: does any of that noise carry real predictive signal about where volatility is headed next, or is price history alone already telling you everything price history can tell you?

Building features that respect how markets actually work

The target was next-period realised volatility — a 12-period rolling standard deviation of log returns, shifted forward so the model is always predicting something it hasn't seen yet. Getting the input features right mattered more than any single model choice:

Beyond lagged returns and rolling volatility, the sentiment features weren't just "sentiment score" on its own —  combines sentiment polarity with mention volume, on the theory that a mildly negative sentiment score attached to a huge spike in social chatter means something different than the same score on a quiet day. Price-based features (momentum, rolling EMA, volume and market-cap on a log scale) sat alongside the sentiment ones so every model saw both signal types and could weight them however the data actually supported.

Four models, one evaluation protocol

GARCH(1,1) — the econometric standard for volatility clustering, and the baseline every other approach has to justify beating. It only sees the return series itself, no sentiment or cross-sectional features at all.

title: Turning Raw Transactional Data Into 100+ Model-Ready Features
description: Notes from building reusable cleansing, validation, and feature-engineering pipelines on 500GB+ of daily enterprise data at Tata Consultancy Services.
content:
At Tata Consultancy Services, a lot of the ML and analytics work downstream of our pipelines kept running into the same wall: the data reaching modelers was close to raw. A handful of source-system fields, maybe a join or two, nothing a classification or forecasting model could really sink its teeth into. Every team building something on top of it ended up re-deriving the same rolling averages and lag features from scratch.

Garbage in, garbage out starts with validation

Before any feature engineering is worth doing, the input has to be trustworthy. I built reusable cleansing and validation frameworks that ran schema checks, completeness checks, duplicate detection, and business-rule validation across 1M+ records before anything reached the warehouse or an analytics consumer. Catching a malformed batch here is cheap; catching it after a model has already trained on it is not.

From a dozen raw fields to 100+ engineered ones

With validated data as the foundation, the actual feature-engineering pipelines expanded a handful of raw transactional fields into over 100 model-ready variables — rolling statistics at multiple time windows, categorical interaction terms, and decay-weighted historical aggregates.

Why PySpark, not pandas, at this scale

Pandas is fine until the dataset stops fitting comfortably in memory on one machine. At 500GB+ processed daily, the rolling-window and groupby operations needed to distribute across a cluster — PySpark on Azure Databricks handled that, with the pandas version above standing in as the readable reference implementation of the same logic.

What I'd tell someone starting this today

A feature pipeline is infrastructure, not a one-off script for a single model. The moment a second team needs "rolling volatility by category," you're better off with one validated, reusable pipeline than three slightly different copies scattered across notebooks. title: Building an NLP Pipeline to Extract Clinical Insights from Medical Text
description: A look at the Intelligent Medical Text Analyser — combining NLTK, SpaCy, and BERT to turn unstructured clinical narratives into structured, searchable insight.
content:
Clinical narratives are some of the messiest unstructured text you can work with — inconsistent abbreviations, dense domain vocabulary, and a writing style optimised for the clinician who wrote it, not for a downstream model. The Intelligent Medical Text Analyser started as a personal project to see how far a layered NLP pipeline could get toward making that text actually searchable.

Why one model wasn't enough

The obvious approach is "throw a transformer at it." That works for some of the pipeline, but not all of it. Classification benefits from a fine-tuned BERT model that's actually seen clinical phrasing. Summarisation over long narratives needs a different strategy than a single-pass classifier. And a lot of the entity extraction — medication names, dosages, symptom mentions — is well served by classic rule-based NLP that's faster and more auditable than a black-box model, which matters a lot in a clinical context.

So the pipeline ended up layered:

Summarisation had a different failure mode

Clinical notes tend to bury the actually-important line — a change in medication, a new symptom — somewhere in the middle of routine documentation. Naive extractive summarisation (just pulling the "most central" sentences by TF-IDF similarity) reliably missed these, because routine documentation is, definitionally, similar to itself across many notes. What worked better was weighting sentences that introduced entities not present in the patient's prior notes — novelty, not centrality, was the signal that mattered.

Where Scikit-learn still earned its place

Not every stage needed deep learning. Triage-style classification — is this note urgent, routine, or follow-up — was well served by a Scikit-learn model over TF-IDF features, and it was fast enough to run on every note rather than sampling.

The Streamlit layer mattered more than expected

title: Can AI Handle Bank Support Tickets Without Making Things Up?
description: Building NovaBank — an AI system that classifies support tickets across 77 banking intents, flags SLA risk before it happens, and answers policy questions without ever inventing a policy that doesn't exist.
content:
Customer support at a bank has three different problems hiding inside one ticket queue: what is this person actually asking?, is this one about to breach its SLA?, and what does policy actually say here? Most support-automation demos solve one of these and wave at the other two. I wanted to see what it took to solve all three honestly, without quietly taking shortcuts that only work on a clean demo dataset.

Classical baseline, then the transformer

With BANKING77 (10,003 training examples, 3,080 test examples, 77 classes), I built a TF-IDF + Logistic Regression baseline first, tuned it properly with stratified 3-fold cross-validation and a GridSearch over n-grams and regularization — not as a strawman, but as a genuine bar to clear.

The 3-epoch DistilBERT run actually lost to the classical baseline — the learning curve was still climbing, a clear sign of undertraining rather than a transformer ceiling. Two more epochs closed that gap and then some: a 4.78-point Macro F1 improvement over the tuned classical model. I also ran the same evaluation on a strict zero-overlap test split to rule out leakage between train and test; the numbers barely moved, which is the result you want to see.

Predicting SLA breaches before they happen

The same raw support dataset I'd rejected for intent classification turned out to be unusable for SLA modelling too — 49.3% of "resolved" tickets had negative resolution times, a timestamp logging bug, not a modelling problem I could fix with a better algorithm. So I built a controlled synthetic NovaBank operational dataset instead, with explicit SLA rules (4h for Critical, 8h for High, 24h Medium, 48h Low) and documented risk-generation assumptions, rather than train on data I already knew was broken.

title: Can AI Tell a Phishing Email From a Leaked Password?
description: Fine-tuning RoBERTa to sort sensitive documents into seven security categories — credentials, PII, financial, medical, confidential, malicious, and safe — and beating a strong classical baseline to do it.
content:
Security and compliance teams deal with a constant stream of documents that need the same first question answered: what kind of sensitive thing is this, and how urgently does it need attention? A leaked API key, a phishing attempt, a customer's medical record pasted somewhere it shouldn't be — these all look like "a block of text" to a naive system, but they need completely different handling. ThreatLens is a classifier built to make that first call automatically.

Starting with class imbalance, not a model

The raw labelled data wasn't close to balanced — the malicious category had substantially more examples than medical, which would have quietly taught any model to favor the bigger classes. I sampled 1,300 documents per category for a balanced set of 9,100 documents before training anything, specifically so the eventual accuracy numbers would mean what they claim to mean, rather than reflecting which class happened to be biggest in the raw data.

Split 7,280 / 910 / 910 for train, validation, and test — stratified so all seven categories stayed represented in equal proportion across every split.

RoBERTa's gains were concentrated in exactly the categories you'd expect to be hardest: confidential (precision rose from 95.38% to 93.33% but recall climbed from 95.38% to 96.92%) and safe — the one category defined mostly by the absence of a signal rather than the presence of one, which is the category classical bag-of-words features tend to find the hardest to pin down.

Reading the mistakes, not just the score

98.35% accuracy on a 910-document test set means roughly 15 documents got misclassified. I pulled every one of them and read the actual text rather than treating "15 errors" as a number to report and move past.
